To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the persistence of mispricing is not fully explained by the behavior of arbitrage traders.
the mean reversion of index basis changes is not fully explained by arbitrage trading and that the net arbitrage trading profit is at the level of zero.

(i) the mean reversion of basis changes is consistent with both mean reversion in market liquidity and partial adjustment of the cash market; (ii) arbitrageurs are highly competitive and their net profits are at the zero level; and (iii) some mispricing persistence is related to time-variation in liquidity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the arbitrageurs' behavior affects the persistence of index arbitrage mispricing.
the question of whether the mean reversion observed in stock index basis is induced by arbitrageurs.
the question of why the mispricing persistence exists.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mean reversion is induced by arbitrageurs, and that arbitrageurs are competitive and value the early closing of positions.
the mean reversion is induced by arbitrage, but the persistence of mispricing is not.
arbitrageurs are not able to fully exploit mispricing opportunities, even though the net profit of arbitrageurs is at the competitive zero level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the market is efficient in the long-run, but not in the short-run.
arbitrage trading is not the only force that induces mean reversion in index basis changes.
arbitrageurs are competitive, but not perfect, and that liquidity is a key element in explaining the persistence of basis mispricing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the market is efficient in the long run, but not in the short run.
the market for index arbitrage is highly competitive.
the mean reversion observed in basis changes is due to a combination of arbitrageurs’ trading, liquidity, and partial adjustment.
